name: Cheek fat pad (Bichat) removal

lead: Cheek fat pad (Bichat) removal, also called buccal fat removal or bichectomy, takes out part of the buccal fat pad, a mass of fat deep in the cheek, usually through an incision inside the mouth. The slimmer lower cheek is visible after healing, with hollower cheeks and a clearer cheekbone-to-jaw transition that users link to the ogee curve.

The pad sits between the buccinator muscle and the more superficial masseter and zygomaticus muscles, and it contributes to cheek fullness. Removing some of its volume reduces fullness in the lower cheek, which proponents say reveals cheekbone and jaw structure. The pad is well documented as a surgical flap in mouth and sinus surgery; published outcome data for purely cosmetic removal are limited.

paras: It is a short procedure through the inside of the mouth, usually under local anaesthetic or sedation, with swelling that settles over weeks. It is popular in looksmaxxing communities as a route to hollow cheeks, often considered alongside leanness.

Wikipedia reports a significant risk of injury to the buccal branch of the facial nerve and the parotid duct. Self-performed removal has been described on forums, and other members in those threads warn against it.

angle.text: Buccal fat removal is popular in looksmaxxing communities as a route to hollow cheeks and a more visible cheekbone-to-jaw transition, often tied to the ogee curve. Taking out part of the cheek fat pad slims the lower cheek once healed. Published outcome data for cosmetic removal are limited.

lead: Cheek fat pad (Bichat) removal, also called buccal fat removal or bichectomy, is a surgical procedure in which part or all of the buccal fat pad, an encapsulated mass of fat deep in the cheek, is taken out, usually through the mouth, to reduce fullness of the lower cheek [1]. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a route to hollow cheeks and a more visible cheekbone-to-jaw transition, often alongside the idea of the ogee curve.

The buccal fat pad lies between the buccinator muscle and the more superficial masseter and zygomaticus muscles, and it contributes to cheek hollowing and the nasolabial fold [1]. Surgical literature has mainly studied the pad as a pedicled flap for closing defects between the mouth and maxillary sinus [2][3], and for its regenerative cells [4][5]. A registered trial of an intraoral removal technique has been completed, but its results are not listed among the sources reviewed here [6].

Wikipedia notes that removal may carry a significant risk of injury to the buccal branch of the facial nerve and the parotid duct [1]. Imaging reviews of cosmetic facial procedures also discuss how fat removal and fat-pad changes appear after surgery [7]. Looksmax.org users have also posted accounts of attempted do-it-yourself removal; these are not documented in the research literature and are not described here.
infobox: Facial nerve branch and parotid duct injury [1]

paras: The buccal fat pad is an encapsulated mass of fat on each side of the face, lying deep to the masseter and zygomaticus muscles and next to the buccinator [1]. Descriptions commonly divide it into anterior, intermediate and posterior lobes, with extensions named sublevator, melolabial, buccal and pterygoid, though there is no single agreed nomenclature [1].

It is distinct from the malar fat pad, which sits directly under the cheek skin, and from the jowl fat pads [1]. Proposed functions include aiding suckling in infants, helping the chewing muscles glide, and cushioning facial muscles [1]. The intermediate lobe is reported to lose notable volume between childhood and adulthood [1].

In surgical practice the pad is typically accessed from inside the mouth. The reviewed sources describe the pad mainly as a flap used for closing oroantral communications and in maxillary and palatal surgery, because it is easily reached from the oral cavity [2][3]. A registered trial (NCT03974373) was set up to evaluate postoperative outcomes of an intraoral technique of buccal fat pad removal in 40 participants [6].

A trial registered as NCT03974373, of an intraoral buccal fat pad removal technique with 40 participants, is listed as completed [6]. No published results from it were found among the sources reviewed here. Other literature concerns the pad's use as a surgical flap for oroantral fistula and related surgery [2][3], and laboratory work on stem cells isolated from the pad [4][5]; these studies do not assess cosmetic removal.

Wikipedia states that removal may carry a significant risk of damaging the buccal branch of the facial nerve and the parotid ducts [1]. Reviews of the pad's surgical anatomy discuss its close relationships with these and other structures [3]. The aging literature, including a plastic surgery paper on combined malar and cheek treatment during facelift, discusses facial volume and contour more broadly [8]. Long-term outcome data on cosmetic removal were not found in the sources reviewed here.

On looksmax.org, hollow cheeks are described as depending on bone structure, the masseter and facial fat, and buccal fat removal appears in threads on the ogee curve as one of several surgical or non-surgical options. Some users post accounts of cutting out the pad themselves, and others in the same thread present safer alternatives; the practice is discussed with warnings by other members.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, buccal fat removal is discussed as a way to achieve hollow cheeks and the ogee curve, with debate about who benefits and how risky it is.
